metadata.title: de Broglie Wavelength Scale — Does the Ruler Actually Work?

beats.narration_text: Bonjour, Liam. Claude built this de Broglie wavelength scale. Our job today is not to teach quantum mechanics — it's to judge whether this visualization does what a visualization should do.

props.command: Hey Claude, write me a visualization for the de Broglie wavelength scale.
output: ✓ log-log λ vs E chart with slope annotation

beats.narration_text: The formula lives in the header: lambda equals h-over-p, or h-over-root-2mK. Below it, a ruler spanning thirty decades of wavelength — ten to the negative thirty-six meters to ten to the negative six. Controls sit in the middle: a mass slider, an energy slider, four presets. To the right: the computed wavelength in large red text, a diffraction flag, and a four-box info grid. The bottom panel is a log-log plot of lambda versus energy.

The mass slider is the primary control. It spans from electron mass — nine-by-ten-to-the-minus-thirty-one kilograms — to human mass at seventy kilograms. The formula says lambda equals h over root-2-m-K. As mass rises, wavelength falls as the square root. Watch the ruler pointer walk left: out of the diffractable zone, through borderline, into classical, and eventually into values that no physical instrument can measure.

Three encodings work. The ruler's color zones carry redundant labels — both fill color and text. A colorblind student reads 'DIFFRACTABLE' in ink; they don't need the red. The log-log chart labels its slope: the dashed segment marked 'slope equals negative one-half' encodes lambda-proportional-to-E-to-the-minus-half as a visible fact. And the info box shows lambda divided by d-Si, the silicon lattice spacing — the diffraction threshold expressed as a ratio, not just a pointer on a ruler.
beats.new_visual_element: Freeze at t=2s: baseline electron 54 eV — DIFFRACTABLE zone pointer, slope annotation, λ/d_Si info box

beats.narration_text: Three encodings fail. The ruler labels only every third decade. Between labeled ticks, there are no numbers — a student cannot read the wavelength at a reference marker without mental arithmetic. The seventy-kilogram one-meter-per-second preset triggers a hidden velocity mode: neither toggle button highlights, the velocity slider appears without announcement, and once the student clicks another preset, it's gone. Finally: the diffraction zone boundary is pinned exclusively to silicon lattice spacing. A student could reasonably conclude diffraction requires silicon.
beats.new_visual_element: Freeze at t=11s: human mass state — 1.9e-26 m, 'Classically negligible', pointer off left of zone

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Three-zone ruler with redundant text labels. Log-log slope annotation makes the power law legible. Lambda-over-d-Si ratio frames the diffraction threshold correctly. The one fix that matters: make the velocity mode reachable through the toggle. Right now the human preset is a black-box button, not an explorable slider.

artifactLines: Three-zone ruler with redundant text labels
Log-log slope annotation makes the power law legible
λ/d_Si ratio frames the diffraction threshold correctly
Fix: expose velocity mode as a real toggle

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Open this simulation and extend it. First, add a Fixed Velocity toggle button beside Fixed Energy and Thermal, with a velocity slider mapping from zero-point-zero-one meters per second to ten thousand meters per second on a log scale. Second, label the ruler axis at every decade — not just every third. Third, rename the lambda-over-d-Si box to lambda-over-d-crystal and add a note explaining that silicon is one example of typical lattice spacings. Keep everything in one HTML file with D3 from CDN.

props.command: Open this de Broglie wavelength scale simulation and extend it. 1. Add a Fixed Velocity toggle beside Fixed Energy and Thermal, with a velocity slider mapping 0.01–10,000 m/s on a log scale. 2. Label the ruler axis at every decade — not just every third. 3. Rename the λ/d_Si box to λ/d_crystal and add a note: 'Si (111) d = 0.31 nm is one example of typical lattice spacings.' Keep one HTML file, D3 from CDN.

beats.narration_text: de Broglie Wavelength Scale, judged. Liam, at NikBearBrown.
